Archaeological hoaxster Charles Dawson excavating the site where he "discovered" the missing link Piltdown Man; with colleagues and pet goose Chipper. East Sussex, England. 1913

Charles Dawson (1864 – 1916) (sitting) was an amateur archaeologist who gained acclaim for his uncanny knack of making spectacular discoveries. He was initially credited with, and is now blamed for, discoveries that turned out to be imaginative frauds.

Most famously, Dawson claimed to have discovered a missing link between humans and other great apes from 500,000 years ago and named it Piltdown Man, or Eoanthropus dawsoni ("Dawson's dawn-man"). The significance of the find remained the subject of considerable controversy until it was conclusively exposed in 1953 as a forgery. It was found to have consisted of the altered jaw and some teeth of an orangutan combined with the skull of a fully developed, though small-brained, modern human.

The Piltdown hoax is prominent for two reasons: the attention it generated around the subject of human evolution, and the length of time, 45 years, that elapsed from its alleged initial discovery to its definitive exposure as a composite forgery.
